title: Representing Data
kicker: Cambridge Lower Secondary · Mathematics 0862 · Stage 8 · Statistics and Probability
summary: Organise and show data with Venn and Carroll diagrams, two-way tables, dual and compound bar charts, pie charts, frequency diagrams, time series, scatter graphs, stem-and-leaf diagrams and infographics — and choose the right one and explain why.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: **Record, organise and represent** categorical, discrete and continuous data, and **choose and explain** which representation to use: Venn and Carroll diagrams; tally charts, frequency tables and two-way tables; dual and compound bar charts; pie charts; frequency diagrams for continuous data; line graphs and time series graphs; scatter graphs; stem-and-leaf diagrams; infographics (8Ss.03)

blocks.text: There are many ways to show data. Checkpoint-style questions ask you to **complete** a table or chart, **read** values from one, and — at Stage 8 — **choose** the best representation and **explain why**. The key question is always: **what type of data is it, and what do I want the reader to see?**
Key words

التكرار — how many times a value or group occurs

سلسلة زمنية — data recorded over time, plotted as points joined by lines

blocks.text: 1. Sorting: Venn and Carroll diagrams

A **Venn diagram** sorts items into sets drawn as overlapping circles inside a rectangle (the universal set, ξ). Items in the overlap belong to **both** sets; items outside the circles belong to **neither**. Below, ξ = the whole numbers 1 to 12, A = multiples of 2 and B = multiples of 3.

blocks.text: A **Carroll diagram** sorts by two properties using a grid. Each property has a column (or row) for “yes” and one for “not”. Here are the same numbers 1 to 12:

Venn and Carroll diagrams can also show **counts** instead of the items themselves. If 40 students were asked, 18 play football, 15 play basketball and 6 play both, the Venn regions are: football only 18 − 6 = 12, both 6, basketball only 15 − 6 = 9, neither 40 − (12 + 6 + 9) = 13. **Always fill the overlap first.**
2. Tally charts, frequency tables and two-way tables

A **tally chart** records data as you collect it (groups of five: four lines and a line across). A **frequency table** gives the totals. For continuous data use **class intervals** with inequalities so that every value fits in exactly one class: 10 ≤ h < 15 means h is at least 10 but less than 15, so a plant of exactly 15 cm goes in the next class.

A **two-way table** shows two categorical variables at the same time. Rows and columns have **totals**, and the grand total is in the bottom-right corner. To fill gaps, use: (row total) = sum of the row, (column total) = sum of the column.

The bold numbers were missing and were worked out: Boys bus = 35 − 12 − 8 = 15; Girls walk = 26 − 12 = 14; Girls total = 14 + 10 + 9 = 33; Bus total = 15 + 10 = 25; Car total = 8 + 9 = 17; grand total = 35 + 33 = 68 (check: 26 + 25 + 17 = 68 ✓).

blocks.text: A **dual** bar chart is best for comparing the groups category by category. A **compound** bar chart is best when the **totals** matter as well as how each total is made up. To read the top part of a compound bar, subtract: football for 8B = 20 − 12 = 8.
4. Pie charts
A **pie chart** shows how a **whole** is shared between categories — the **proportions**. The full circle is 360°.

items: Find the total frequency. Example: 36 students said how they travel to school.
Find the angle for one item: 360° ÷ 36 = 10° per student.
Multiply each frequency: walk 9 × 10° = 90°, bus 15 × 10° = 150°, car 10 × 10° = 100°, bicycle 2 × 10° = 20°.
Check the angles add up to 360°: 90 + 150 + 100 + 20 = 360 ✓.
Draw a radius, measure each angle with a protractor from the last line, and label every sector (or use a key).

blocks.text: **Reading a pie chart:** number in a sector = (angle ÷ 360) × total. If 120 people are shown and a sector is 75°, it shows 75 ÷ 360 × 120 = 25 people. A pie chart shows **proportions**, not actual numbers — two pie charts of different-sized groups cannot be compared by sector size alone.
5. Frequency diagrams for continuous data

Continuous data (heights, masses, times) are grouped into **equal class intervals** and drawn as a **frequency diagram**: like a bar chart but with **no gaps** between the bars, and a **continuous scale** on the horizontal axis (numbers at the edges of the bars, not under the middle).

blocks.text: 6. Line graphs and time series

When data are recorded **over time** (each month, each year, every hour), draw a **time series graph**: time on the horizontal axis, plot each value and join the points with straight lines. It shows **trends** (going up or down overall) and **seasonal patterns** (repeating ups and downs). The lines between points only show the change; values between the points are not measured.

8. Stem-and-leaf diagrams

A **stem-and-leaf diagram** keeps every data value **and** shows the shape of the data. For two-digit numbers, the **stem** is the tens digit and the **leaf** is the units digit. Leaves are written **in order** and lined up, and there must be a **key**. Times (seconds) of 15 students to solve a puzzle: 23, 27, 31, 34, 34, 38, 40, 42, 45, 45, 47, 51, 53, 58, 62.

Key: 3|4 means 34 seconds. From the diagram you can read the smallest value (23), the largest (62), the mode (34 and 45 both appear twice) and count values — for example, 8 students took less than 45 seconds.
9. Infographics, and choosing a representation

An **infographic** combines pictures, icons, big numbers, short text and simple charts to tell a story with data quickly, e.g. a school poster: “3 out of 4 students walk or cycle” with 4 student icons, 3 of them shaded. Infographics are eye-catching, but check them: are the icons the same size? Is the scale shown? Is the source given?

blocks.text: Worked examples

**Worked example 1** — Two-way table  [2 marks]
In a group of 50 students, 28 are girls. 19 of the girls and 12 of the boys have a pet. How many students do **not** have a pet?

items: Have a pet = 19 + 12 = 31.
No pet = 50 − 31 = 19. (Check by parts: girls with no pet 28 − 19 = 9; boys with no pet 22 − 12 = 10; 9 + 10 = 19 ✓)

blocks.text:
**Answer:** 19 students.
**Common mistake:** subtracting 31 from 28 or 22 instead of from the grand total.

**Worked example 2** — Pie chart angle  [2 marks]
60 people chose their favourite drink. 18 chose tea. Work out the angle of the sector for tea.

360° ÷ 60 = 6° per person. 18 × 6° = 108°.
**Answer:** 108°. (1 mark for 6° per person or 18/60 × 360 seen.)
**Common mistake:** using 100 instead of 360, giving 30 — that is the percentage, not the angle.

**Worked example 3** — Reading a pie chart  [1 mark]
A pie chart shows the favourite fruit of 120 people. The sector for mango has an angle of 75°. How many people chose mango?

**Worked example 4** — Venn diagram  [2 marks]
Of 40 students, 18 play football, 15 play basketball and 6 play both. How many play neither?

Football only = 18 − 6 = 12. Basketball only = 15 − 6 = 9. At least one sport = 12 + 6 + 9 = 27. Neither = 40 − 27 = 13.
**Answer:** 13.
**Common mistake:** 40 − 18 − 15 = 7. This counts the 6 students who play both sports twice.

**Worked example 5** — Choosing a representation  [2 marks]
Amira recorded the height and the arm span of 20 students. She wants to see whether taller students have longer arm spans. Which diagram should she draw? Explain why.

**Answer:** a **scatter graph** (1 mark), because it shows the relationship (correlation) between two sets of numerical data from the same students (1 mark).
**Common mistake:** choosing a bar chart or pie chart; these show one variable only.

**Worked example 6** — Stem-and-leaf  [2 marks]
Draw an ordered stem-and-leaf diagram for these marks: 34, 52, 41, 38, 45, 29, 52, 47, 33, 40.

items: Add a key, for example 4|5 means 45 marks.

blocks.text:
**Answer:** as above (1 mark for correct leaves, 1 mark for ordered with a key).
**Common mistake:** forgetting the key, or not putting the leaves in order (an unordered diagram usually loses a mark).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Leaving gaps between the bars of a frequency diagram for continuous data — or no gaps on a bar chart for categories.
Writing class intervals that overlap (10–15, 15–20). Use 10 ≤ h < 15, 15 ≤ h < 20.
Pie chart angles that do not add up to 360°; or measuring each angle from the same starting line instead of from the previous sector.
Comparing two pie charts of different-sized groups as if the sectors showed numbers.
Reading the top part of a compound bar from zero instead of subtracting.
Forgetting the key or the ordering in a stem-and-leaf diagram.
Saying scatter-graph correlation proves that one variable causes the other.
In a Venn diagram, filling the circles before the overlap, so the “both” items are counted twice.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: “Complete the two-way table” or “Complete the Venn/Carroll diagram” — fill the given totals first, then subtract.
“Complete the pie chart” — show 360 ÷ total; draw angles accurately (±2°) and label each sector.
“Draw a frequency diagram” or “complete the time series graph” on a printed grid — plot exactly, join time series points with straight lines.
“What type of correlation …?” and “Describe the relationship” — use the context words.
“Which diagram would you use? Give a reason.” — name the diagram and say what it shows (proportion, comparison, change over time, relationship).
“Draw an ordered stem-and-leaf diagram” — include a key.

questions.q: Hana wants to show how the number of visitors to a museum changed each month over two years. (a) Name the best type of graph. (b) Explain why a pie chart would not be suitable.
questions.ms: 1 mark: time series graph (accept line graph). 1 mark: a pie chart shows proportions of a whole / cannot show change or trend over time / 24 sectors would be hard to read. Do not accept “a pie chart is too hard to draw” alone.
questions.e: (a) A time series (line) graph, with the months along the horizontal axis, shows how the numbers change over time and any trend or seasonal pattern. (b) A pie chart only shows how a total is shared out; it does not show the order of the months or how the visitors increase or decrease.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Categorical/discrete data: bar charts with gaps — dual to compare groups, compound to show totals and parts.
Pie charts show proportions: angle = frequency × (360 ÷ total); angles add up to 360°.
Continuous data: equal class intervals with inequalities and a frequency diagram with no gaps.
Time series show change over time; scatter graphs show correlation (positive, negative, none) — not cause.
Venn and two-way tables: fill the overlap or given totals first, then subtract. Stem-and-leaf: ordered leaves and a key.
When asked to choose, name the diagram and say what it shows in the context.
